title: Voltage, current, resistance, power, energy
summary: The four quantities every circuit is described by.

layers.basics: Voltage is the push, current is the flow, resistance is the opposition and power is how fast energy is used.
layers.deeper: Conventional current flows from + to − through a load and from − to + inside a source; a component absorbs power when current enters its + terminal. Energy bills are watts × time.
layers.expert: Passive sign convention; P=VI; units V, A, Ω, W, J (=W·s); a kilowatt-hour is 3.6 MJ. Ideal sources and ground reference define the model world of lumped circuits.

title: Ohm’s law
summary: V = I·R for a resistor.

layers.basics: The current through a resistor is proportional to the voltage across it.
layers.deeper: A resistor’s I–V line is straight; non-ohmic devices (diodes, lamps) curve. Resistors dissipate P=I²R as heat.
layers.expert: Ohm’s law is an empirical relation, J=σE, valid over a wide but limited range; σ changes with temperature, and diodes are non-ohmic.

formula: V = I R;  P = I²R = V²/R

title: Kirchhoff’s current law (KCL)
summary: Currents into a node sum to zero.

layers.basics: Charge does not pile up at a junction: what flows in must flow out.
layers.deeper: KCL gives one equation per node, but only N−1 of them are independent in a connected circuit with N nodes; it is charge conservation applied to a node.
layers.expert: Σiₖ=0 on any closed surface for lumped circuits; displacement current extends it to capacitors in Maxwell’s form.

title: Kirchhoff’s voltage law (KVL)
summary: Voltage drops around a loop sum to zero.

layers.basics: Go around any closed loop and the rises and drops in voltage must cancel.
layers.deeper: KVL gives one equation per independent loop and is energy conservation per unit charge.
layers.expert: Σvₖ=0 around closed paths if no time-varying flux links the loop; otherwise lumped models add an inductor.

title: Series and parallel circuits
summary: Two basic ways to connect components.

layers.basics: Series elements share the same current; parallel elements share the same voltage.
layers.deeper: Resistances add in series and conductances add in parallel; capacitors do the opposite of resistors, inductors the same.
layers.expert: R_series=ΣRᵢ; 1/R_par=Σ1/Rᵢ; reductions of ladders step by step; Y–Δ conversion for bridge-type networks.

title: Voltage divider
summary: Two resistors split a voltage.

layers.basics: Two series resistors share a voltage in proportion to their sizes, giving a smaller voltage at the middle.
layers.deeper: Loading the output changes the ratio; used in sensor interfaces, bias networks and ADC inputs.
layers.expert: Vout=Vin R₂/(R₁+R₂) unloaded; with load, replace R₂ by R₂∥R_L; Thévenin equivalent R₁∥R₂.

title: Current divider
summary: Parallel branches split a current.

layers.basics: Current prefers the easier path: the smaller resistor takes more of it.
layers.deeper: Used in ammeter shunts, which divert most of the current around the meter movement, and in analysing parallel loads.
layers.expert: I₁=I_T R₂/(R₁+R₂) for two branches; for n branches I_k=I_T G_k/ΣG.

title: Nodal analysis
summary: Solve for node voltages with KCL.

layers.basics: Pick a ground, label the other node voltages, and write KCL at each node; then solve the equations.
layers.deeper: In matrix form G·v=i with G the conductance matrix; supernodes handle floating voltage sources.
layers.expert: Modified nodal analysis (MNA) adds branch currents for voltage sources and inductors; it is the engine of SPICE.

title: Mesh analysis
summary: Solve for loop currents with KVL.

layers.basics: Assign a current to each window of a planar circuit and write KVL around it.
layers.deeper: Meshes sharing a branch couple through that resistor; supermeshes handle current sources.
layers.expert: R·i=v for planar circuits with R_ii the mesh resistance and R_ij the shared (negative) one; dual of nodal analysis.

title: Superposition
summary: Linear circuits respond to each source separately.

layers.basics: Compute the effect of each source alone (others turned off) and add the results.
layers.deeper: Turn off voltage sources by shorting them and current sources by opening. It fails for power, which is non-linear.
layers.expert: Holds for any linear circuit; used to split AC and DC and to superpose different frequencies.

title: Thévenin and Norton equivalents
summary: Any linear one-port is a source plus a resistor.

layers.basics: Any linear two-terminal circuit can be replaced with a single voltage source in series with a resistor (or a current source in parallel).
layers.deeper: Find V_th as the open-circuit voltage and R_th by turning sources off. Great for analysing loads and amplifier outputs.
layers.expert: V_th=I_N R_th; extends to impedances Z_th; test-source method works with dependent sources.

title: Maximum power transfer
summary: A load takes most power when matched to the source.

layers.basics: A load gets the greatest power when its resistance equals the source’s internal resistance.
layers.deeper: For a source modelled as a fixed Thévenin voltage behind a resistance, matching delivers only half the source power to the load (50% efficiency), so power systems avoid it; radio links match impedances to avoid reflections on the line, though real transmitters are not simple Thévenin sources.
layers.expert: P_L=V_th²R_L/(R_th+R_L)² peaks at R_L=R_th; for AC, Z_L=Z_th* (conjugate match).

title: Source transformations
summary: Swap a voltage source+R for a current source+R.

layers.basics: A voltage source in series with a resistor behaves the same as a current source in parallel with it, so you can swap them to simplify.
layers.deeper: The transformation is a quick pencil-and-paper way to combine sources; only the outside terminals match.
layers.expert: I_s=V_s/R_s with the same R_s in parallel (R_s must be non-zero and finite); only the terminal behaviour matches, not internal dissipation; with dependent sources it needs care, because the controlling variable must not be lost in the transformation.

title: Dependent (controlled) sources
summary: Sources whose value depends on another voltage or current.

layers.basics: Transistors and op-amps act like sources controlled by an input, so analysing them needs dependent sources in the circuit model.
layers.deeper: Four types: VCVS, VCCS, CCVS, CCCS; keep the control variable in the equations, don’t turn the source off in superposition.
layers.expert: Small-signal BJT: i_c=β i_b (CCCS) or g_m v_be (VCCS); gains of ideal amplifiers are VCVS parameters.

title: Capacitor in circuits
summary: Stores energy in an electric field.

layers.basics: A capacitor blocks steady DC but passes changing signals; it holds a charge.
layers.deeper: Current is proportional to the rate of change of voltage; the voltage cannot jump. Used for decoupling, filtering, timing.
layers.expert: i=C dv/dt; impedance 1/(jωC); real capacitors add ESR, ESL and leakage; capacitor types (C0G and X7R ceramic, aluminium electrolytic) differ in stability, loss and voltage dependence.

title: Inductor in circuits
summary: Stores energy in a magnetic field.

layers.basics: An inductor resists changes in current; it passes steady DC and opposes fast changes.
layers.deeper: Voltage is proportional to the rate of change of current; the current cannot jump. Switching an inductor off produces a voltage spike.
layers.expert: v=L di/dt; impedance jωL; real inductors saturate and have winding resistance and parasitic capacitance; flyback spikes are tamed with diodes or snubbers.

title: RC transient response
summary: Exponential charging and discharging.

layers.basics: When a capacitor charges through a resistor, the voltage rises fast then levels off; the time constant is R×C.
layers.deeper: After one time constant the capacitor is 63% charged; after five it is effectively full. Used for timers, debouncing and filters.
layers.expert: v(t)=V_f+(V_0−V_f)e^{−t/τ}, τ=RC. Charging an initially empty capacitor to a source voltage V, the source delivers CV²: half is stored and half is dissipated in R, whatever R is.

title: RL transient response
summary: Current builds up gradually in a coil.

layers.basics: After a switch closes, current in a coil climbs towards its final value V/R with time constant L/R: about 63% of the way after one L/R.
layers.deeper: It mirrors the RC case with current and voltage roles swapped.
layers.expert: i(t)=I_f+(I₀−I_f)e^{−tR/L}; opening a switch on an inductive load forces large di/dt unless a path is provided.

title: RLC natural and step response
summary: Ringing circuits.

layers.basics: A circuit with R, L and C can oscillate as energy sloshes between capacitor and inductor, while R drains it.
layers.deeper: The damping ratio ζ=(R/2)·√(C/L)=α/ω₀ of a series RLC circuit decides whether the response overshoots and rings (ζ<1) or creeps to its final value (ζ>1).
layers.expert: Characteristic roots s=−α±√(α²−ω₀²); ω₀=1/√(LC), and α=R/2L for the series circuit (α=1/2RC for the parallel circuit). Natural response (no source) and step response (DC drive) share roots, differ by forced term.

title: Overdamped, underdamped and critically damped
summary: Three flavours of second-order response.

layers.basics: Overdamped: slow smooth return. Underdamped: oscillating and decaying. Critically damped: the fastest return without ringing.
layers.deeper: α>ω₀ gives two real roots, α=ω₀ a double root, α<ω₀ complex roots with damped frequency ω_d.
layers.expert: Q=ω₀/2α; underdamped overshoot exp(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)); for the underdamped case the 2% settling time is ≈4/α; critical damping is a design target for sensors and shock absorbers.

title: Sinusoidal AC and phasors
summary: Steady alternating signals as complex numbers.

layers.basics: Mains power is a sine wave. Phasors let you handle amplitude and phase with simple complex arithmetic.
layers.deeper: In the phasor domain, inductors and capacitors behave like complex resistors; Kirchhoff and Ohm still apply.
layers.expert: v=Vm cos(ωt+φ) ↔ V=Vm∠φ; ω=2πf; phase leads and lags; valid for linear steady-state.

title: Impedance and admittance
summary: Resistance generalised to AC.

layers.basics: Impedance Z combines resistance and reactance; it says how much a component opposes AC and shifts its phase.
layers.deeper: Z_R=R, Z_L=jωL, Z_C=1/(jωC). Admittance Y=1/Z is handy in parallel circuits.
layers.expert: Z=R+jX; |Z|=√(R²+X²); series impedances add, parallel admittances add; Kirchhoff’s laws hold unchanged for phasors.

title: RMS and average power
summary: The DC-equivalent of an AC waveform.

layers.basics: RMS (root-mean-square) tells the DC value that would heat a resistor equally. Mains of 230 V RMS peaks at 325 V.
layers.deeper: Average power in a resistor is V_rms·I_rms; reactive elements store and return energy without net consumption.
layers.expert: V_rms=√(1/T∫v²dt); for a sine Vm/√2; for non-sinusoids use true-RMS meters.

title: Real, reactive and complex power
summary: P, Q and S: what is used, what sloshes, what is carried.

layers.basics: Real power P does work; reactive power Q flows back and forth; apparent power S is the product V_rms·I_rms.
layers.deeper: S=P+jQ with units W, var and VA; the power triangle relates them; conductors, transformers and generators are sized on VA because they must carry the full current, including the part that does no work.
layers.expert: With rms phasors, S=VI*; P=|V||I|cosφ, Q=|V||I|sinφ, φ=arg V − arg I. With associated reference directions, Tellegen’s theorem makes the complex powers of all elements sum to zero.

title: Power factor and correction
summary: How efficiently current is used.

layers.basics: Power factor is the fraction of apparent power that does real work. Motors lower it; capacitors bring it back.
layers.deeper: Low PF means extra current, extra line losses and bigger cables; factories add capacitor banks.
layers.expert: In general pf=P/S=displacement factor × distortion factor; for sinusoidal waveforms pf=cosφ. Single-phase correction capacitance (V = rms load voltage): C=P(tanφ₁−tanφ₂)/(ωV²); non-linear loads add distortion PF, solved by PFC converters.

title: Three-phase circuits (wye and delta)
summary: Three sinusoids 120° apart.

layers.basics: Three-phase power uses three conductors carrying sine waves offset by 120°, with a balanced load the total instantaneous power is constant, and less conductor is needed than for single-phase at the same power.
layers.deeper: Wye (star) and delta connections link sources and loads: line voltage is √3 times phase voltage in wye.
layers.expert: For a balanced load, P_total=√3 V_L I_L cosφ with φ the angle between phase voltage and phase current; balanced systems analysed per-phase; unbalanced via symmetrical components; rotating field for motors.

title: Transfer functions
summary: Output over input as a function of frequency.

layers.basics: A transfer function H tells how a circuit scales and shifts each frequency.
layers.deeper: It is a ratio of polynomials in s; its poles set natural responses.
layers.expert: H(s)=Vout(s)/Vin(s); for impedance-based networks follow from divider formulas with Z(s).

title: Frequency response and Bode plots
summary: Gain and phase on log axes.

layers.basics: A Bode plot shows gain (in dB) and phase against log frequency, revealing a circuit’s character at a glance.
layers.deeper: Each pole bends the gain slope by −20 dB/decade and the phase by −90° (over a decade or two).
layers.expert: Asymptotic approximation: corner at ω=1/τ, −3 dB there and −45° phase; composite plots by adding contributions of poles and zeros.

title: Resonance and quality factor
summary: Tuning and sharpness.

layers.basics: An RLC circuit responds strongly near one frequency, its resonance; Q measures how narrow the peak is.
layers.deeper: Radio tuners pick one station using this. High Q means narrow bandwidth and long ringing.
layers.expert: ω₀=1/√LC; series Q=ω₀L/R; bandwidth B=ω₀/Q; at resonance reactances cancel, series Z=R.

title: Low-pass filter
summary: Pass slow, block fast.

layers.basics: A resistor and a capacitor in series, outputting across the capacitor, pass low frequencies and attenuate high ones.
layers.deeper: Cutoff f_c=1/(2πRC); used for anti-aliasing and removing noise.
layers.expert: First-order −20 dB/dec; higher order by cascading or active designs (Butterworth, Chebyshev).

title: High-pass filter
summary: Pass fast, block slow.

layers.basics: Swapping the R and C passes high frequencies and blocks DC.
layers.deeper: Used for AC coupling and removing drift.
layers.expert: H(s)=sRC/(1+sRC); phase leads by up to +90° at low frequency.

title: Band-pass filter
summary: Pass one band.

layers.basics: Combine high- and low-pass sections, or use a resonant circuit, to pass only a band of frequencies.
layers.deeper: Centre f₀ and bandwidth set selectivity; radios and EEG front-ends use band-pass stages.
layers.expert: Second-order H=(ω₀/Q)s/(s²+(ω₀/Q)s+ω₀²).

title: Notch (band-stop) filter
summary: Remove one frequency.

layers.basics: A notch filter blocks a narrow band, such as 50/60 Hz mains hum, and passes everything else.
layers.deeper: Twin-T and bridged networks create the notch; ECG amplifiers reduce mains pickup mainly with shielding, instrumentation amplifiers and a right-leg drive circuit; a notch can add to that.
layers.expert: Zeros on jω axis at ω₀ with Q controlling width; digital notches use z-plane zeros on the unit circle.

title: Two-port networks
summary: Black-box description of a circuit with input and output.

layers.basics: A two-port is characterised by a small matrix relating input and output voltages and currents.
layers.deeper: Z, Y, h, ABCD and S parameters are different ways to write the same relation; cascaded stages multiply ABCD matrices.
layers.expert: Reciprocity (Z12=Z21) holds for networks built only from resistors, capacitors and inductors (including mutual inductance); passive devices containing ferrite, such as circulators and isolators, are non-reciprocal; S-parameters are used at RF where open/short measurement is hard.

title: Mutual inductance
summary: Coupled coils.

layers.basics: Two coils near each other share magnetic flux, so current in one induces voltage in the other.
layers.deeper: The coupling M=k√(L₁L₂); the dot convention gives the sign of the induced voltage.
layers.expert: v₁=L₁di₁/dt+M di₂/dt; leakage inductance and magnetising inductance model non-ideal coupling.

title: Ideal transformer
summary: Changes voltage and current levels.

layers.basics: A transformer swaps voltage for current using two coils on a shared core; V₂/V₁ equals turns ratio.
layers.deeper: Power is preserved; impedances are scaled by the ratio squared; it only works when the current, and so the flux, changes in time: AC or switched DC, never steady DC.
layers.expert: V₂/V₁=N₂/N₁, I₂/I₁=N₁/N₂, Z_in=(N₁/N₂)²Z_L; real transformers have winding resistance, leakage, core loss, saturation.

title: Laplace-domain circuit analysis
summary: Circuits with initial conditions, as algebra.

layers.basics: Replace each element with its s-domain impedance and add small sources for initial conditions; solve like a resistor network.
layers.deeper: It handles transients and non-sinusoidal inputs; inverse transform returns the time response.
layers.expert: Z_R=R, Z_L=sL (+L i₀ source), Z_C=1/sC (+v₀/s source); convolution in time ↔ product in s.
